## 1. Purpose and Scope

This guidance bridges the language-agnostic security patterns in the EAP pattern catalog to concrete Node.js 20 LTS implementations. It targets engineers building Node.js backend APIs and provides working TypeScript code examples for the most common security integration points.

**Normative baseline**: All content here implements requirements from [STD-TEC-NODE-001](../../../../standards/technology/nodejs/STD-TEC-NODE-001-security.md). Where this guidance provides a code example, that example is a reference implementation of the corresponding standard requirement — not an alternative to it.

**Out of scope**: Frontend Node.js tooling (Webpack, Vite), server-side rendering, and CLI tooling. See [GUID-TEC-NODE-002](../../application/nodejs/GUID-TEC-NODE-002-bff-implementation.md) for Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) guidance.

## 2. Framework Selection

Three frameworks are approved for Node.js backend microservices at Gainwell Technologies. Each requires the security middleware stack defined in STD-TEC-NODE-001 §3, but the configuration approach differs per framework.
page_texts.8:
[strategy/guidance/security/nodejs/GUID-TEC-NODE-001-secure-microservice-implementation.md#24-selection-guidance]

### 2.4 Selection Guidance

| Use Case | Recommended Framework |
|---|---|
| Simple CRUD API with 3–5 resources | Express |
| High-throughput data pipeline or aggregation API | Fastify |
| Complex service with 5+ domain modules, DI required | NestJS |
| Existing Express service — do not rewrite unless justified | Express |

Do not choose a framework solely on familiarity. The selection must be recorded in the service's ADR.

[strategy/guidance/security/nodejs/GUID-TEC-NODE-001-secure-microservice-implementation.md#3-typescript-enforcement]

## 3. TypeScript Enforcement

TypeScript is **required**. The rationale is not stylistic — it is operational:

- Type errors in healthcare data mapping (e.g., treating a nullable `memberId` as a non-nullable string) surface at compile time rather than in production.
- TypeScript's `strict` mode eliminates the most common class of `null`/`undefined` runtime errors.
- Explicit return types on service and controller functions serve as executable documentation of contracts.

The mandatory `tsconfig.json` is defined in [STD-TEC-NODE-002 §2.2](../../../../standards/technology/nodejs/STD-TEC-NODE-002-coding.md). The key options that must not be weakened:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noImplicitAny": true,
    "strictNullChecks": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "skipLibCheck": false
  }
}
```

`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is particularly important for healthcare data processing: accessing `array[index]` returns `T | undefined` rather than `T`, forcing explicit null handling when iterating over arrays of claim lines, eligibility records, or provider results.

## 5. Project Structure Conventions

All Node.js microservices must follow the directory structure defined in [STD-TEC-NODE-002 §6](../../../../standards/technology/nodejs/STD-TEC-NODE-002-coding.md). The structure reflects the bounded context boundaries required by STD-APP-API-002:

```text
member-service/
├── src/
│   ├── api/                     # HTTP boundary (controllers, middleware, routes)
│   │   ├── controllers/
│   │   │   └── member.controller.ts
│   │   ├── middleware/
│   │   │   ├── auth.middleware.ts
│   │   │   ├── correlation-id.middleware.ts
│   │   │   └── error-handler.middleware.ts
│   │   └── routes/
│   │       ├── members.router.ts
│   │       └── health.router.ts
│   ├── domain/                  # Business logic (no HTTP imports)
│   │   ├── models/
│   │   │   └── member.model.ts
│   │   ├── services/
│   │   │   └── member.service.ts
│   │   └── repositories/
│   │       └── member.repository.ts  # Interface only
│   ├── infrastructure/          # External integrations
│   │   ├── db/
│   │   │   └── member.db-repository.ts
│   │   ├── http/
│   │   │   └── eligibility.client.ts
│   │   └── secrets/
│   │       └── aws-secrets.client.ts
│   ├── config/
│   │   └── index.ts
│   ├── utils/
│   │   ├── async-route.ts
│   │   ├── errors.ts
│   │   ├── logger.ts
│   │   └── sanitise-log-body.ts
│   ├── app.ts
│   └── server.ts
├── tests/
├── .eslintrc.cjs
├── .nvmrc
├── .prettierrc
├── package.json
├── package-lock.json
└── tsconfig.json
```

[strategy/guidance/security/nodejs/GUID-TEC-NODE-001-secure-microservice-implementation.md#7-container-security-cross-reference]

## 7. Container Security Cross-Reference

Node.js services are deployed as container images. The following container-level controls complement the application-level controls in this guidance:

- **Distroless base image**: Use `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12` or `node:20-slim`. Full OS images (`node:20`) include package managers and shells that expand the attack surface. See [GUID-SEC-APPS-CONTAINER-SECURITY-2.7.05](../../Application/GUID-SEC-APPS-CONTAINER-SECURITY-2.7.05.md) for the full container hardening policy.
- **`npm ci` in Dockerfile**: Use `npm ci --omit=dev` in the production image build stage to exclude development dependencies from the container layer.
- **Non-root user**: Run the Node.js process as a non-root user:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-slim AS production
WORKDIR /app
RUN addgroup --system nodegroup && adduser --system --ingroup nodegroup nodeuser
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
USER nodeuser
ENV NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=512"
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

- **Read-only filesystem**: Set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` in the Kubernetes pod security context. Log to stdout/stderr rather than files.
